claim: Imaginal discs of Drosophila are subdivided into distinct compartments, which derive from different genetic programs.
source: The imaginal discs of Drosophila are subdivided into distinct compartments, which derive from different genetic programs.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as established background knowledge about Drosophila imaginal discs.

claim: Massive damage inflicted to the posterior or the dorsal compartment of the wing disc causes a transient breakdown of compartment boundaries.
source: We find that massive damage inflicted to the posterior or the dorsal compartment of the wing disc causes a transient breakdown of compartment boundaries, which are quickly reconstructed.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Compartment boundaries are quickly reconstructed after massive damage.
source: We find that massive damage inflicted to the posterior or the dorsal compartment of the wing disc causes a transient breakdown of compartment boundaries, which are quickly reconstructed.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations.

claim: Cells involved in boundary reconstruction often modify their original identity, visualized by changes in the expression of developmental genes like engrailed or cubitus interruptus.
source: The cells involved in the reconstruction often modify their original identity, visualized by changes in the expression of developmental genes like engrailed or cubitus interruptus.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through immunostaining data in the figures.

claim: Cell reprogramming during regeneration is mediated by up regulation of the JNK pathway.
source: This reprogramming is mediated by up regulation of the JNK pathway and transient debilitation of the epigenetic control mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing JNK activity is required for boundary transgressions.

claim: Cell reprogramming during regeneration is mediated by transient debilitation of the epigenetic control mechanism.
source: This reprogramming is mediated by up regulation of the JNK pathway and transient debilitation of the epigenetic control mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing alterations in Pc-G and trx-G gene activity.

claim: The local developmental context plays a role in the acquisition of new cell identities during regeneration.
source: Our results also show that the local developmental context plays a role in the acquisition of new cell identities: cells expressing engrailed induce engrailed expression in neighbor cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing en induction in neighboring cells.

claim: Cells expressing engrailed induce engrailed expression in neighbor cells.
source: Our results also show that the local developmental context plays a role in the acquisition of new cell identities: cells expressing engrailed induce engrailed expression in neighbor cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through clonal analysis experiments.

claim: In the regeneration of an amputated amphibian limb, proximal cells have to generate new cells with distal identity.
source: In the classical example of the regeneration of an amputated amphibian limb (Kragl et al., 2009), proximal cells have to generate new cells with different—distal—identity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kragl et al., 2009.

claim: Very little is known about the phenomena and mechanisms behind developmental reprogramming during regeneration.
source: Very little is known about the phenomena and mechanisms behind this developmental reprogramming.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The subdivision into lineage blocks, termed compartments, is a principal feature of the organization of the body of Drosophila.
source: The subdivision into lineage blocks, termed compartments, is a principal feature of the organization of the body of Drosophila (Garcia-Bellido et al., 1973; Morata & Lawrence, 1977).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Garcia-Bellido et al., 1973 and Morata & Lawrence, 1977.

claim: The earliest compartmentalization event is established during embryogenesis and separates anterior (A) and posterior (P) compartments in each segment.
source: The earliest compartmentalization event is established during embryogenesis (Lawrence & Morata, 1977) and separates anterior (A) and posterior (P) compartments in each segment.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Lawrence & Morata, 1977.

claim: The A/P boundaries in different body segments are topological landmarks to delimit Hox genes expression.
source: The A/P boundaries in the different body segments not only separate the original lineage blocks of the fly; they also are topological landmarks to delimit Hox genes expression (Lawrence, 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Lawrence, 1992.

claim: P compartments acquire expression of the engrailed (en) gene, which determines anterior or posterior identity within each segment.
source: Since the initial establishment of the A/P boundary, the P compartments acquire expression of the engrailed (en) gene, which determines anterior or posterior identity within each segment: the 'on' state specifies posterior whereas the 'off' state specifies anterior identity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of engrailed in compartment identity.

claim: The 'on' state of engrailed specifies posterior identity whereas the 'off' state specifies anterior identity.
source: Since the initial establishment of the A/P boundary, the P compartments acquire expression of the engrailed (en) gene, which determines anterior or posterior identity within each segment: the 'on' state specifies posterior whereas the 'off' state specifies anterior identity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about engrailed function.

claim: Early lineage segregation is preserved for the rest of development in all larval and adult structures.
source: This early lineage segregation is preserved for the rest of the development in all larval and adult structures.
evidence: This is established knowledge about compartment stability during normal development.

claim: In imaginal discs, engrailed remains expressed in the P compartments.
source: In the imaginal discs (the precursors of the adult cuticular structures) en remains expressed in the P compartments (Brower, 1986) and is also required to maintain the A/P border (Morata and Lawrence, 1975).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Brower, 1986.

claim: Engrailed is required to maintain the A/P border.
source: In the imaginal discs (the precursors of the adult cuticular structures) en remains expressed in the P compartments (Brower, 1986) and is also required to maintain the A/P border (Morata and Lawrence, 1975).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Morata and Lawrence, 1975.

claim: The absence of en function in the A compartment allows anterior cells to activate the Hh pathway and subsequently the cubitus interruptus (ci) gene.
source: The absence of en function in the A compartment allows anterior cells to activate the Hh pathway and subsequently the cubitus interruptus (ci) gene, a marker of A compartment identity (Orenic et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Orenic et al., 1990.

claim: Cubitus interruptus (ci) is a marker of A compartment identity.
source: The absence of en function in the A compartment allows anterior cells to activate the Hh pathway and subsequently the cubitus interruptus (ci) gene, a marker of A compartment identity (Orenic et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Orenic et al., 1990.

claim: The expression of en is regulated epigenetically.
source: The expression of en is regulated epigenetically.
evidence: This is established knowledge about engrailed regulation.

claim: Engrailed is kept in off (silenced) state in the A compartments through the activity of the Polycomb-G genes (Pc-G).
source: It is kept in off (silenced) state in the A compartments through the activity of the Polycomb-G genes (Pc-G) (Busturia and Morata, 1988), whereas the trithorax-G genes (trx-G) maintain en in on state in P compartments (Breen et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Busturia and Morata, 1988.

claim: The trithorax-G genes (trx-G) maintain en in on state in P compartments.
source: It is kept in off (silenced) state in the A compartments through the activity of the Polycomb-G genes (Pc-G) (Busturia and Morata, 1988), whereas the trithorax-G genes (trx-G) maintain en in on state in P compartments (Breen et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Breen et al., 1995.

claim: There is a lineage border in the wing disc separating the dorsal (D) and the ventral (V) compartments.
source: In addition to the A/P boundary, there is in the wing disc another lineage border, separating the dorsal (D) and the ventral (V) compartments.
evidence: This is established knowledge about wing disc organization.

claim: The D/V boundary appears during larval development.
source: This boundary appears during larval development (Garcia-Bellido et al., 1973) and is dependent on the activity of the gene apterous (ap), which confers dorsal identity (Diaz-Benjumea and Cohen, 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Garcia-Bellido et al., 1973.

claim: The D/V boundary is dependent on the activity of the gene apterous (ap), which confers dorsal identity.
source: This boundary appears during larval development (Garcia-Bellido et al., 1973) and is dependent on the activity of the gene apterous (ap), which confers dorsal identity (Diaz-Benjumea and Cohen, 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Diaz-Benjumea and Cohen, 1993.

claim: The A/P and D/V borders function as developmental organizers of the imaginal discs.
source: The A/P and the D/V borders not only separate cells with different identities in the wing disc; they also function as developmental organizers of the imaginal discs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of compartment boundaries.

claim: Posterior compartment cells secrete the Hedgehog (Hh) morphogen that activates the decapentaplegic (dpp) gene in the anterior cells close to the border.
source: The posterior compartment cells secrete the Hedgehog (Hh) morphogen that activates the decapentaplegic (dpp) gene in the anterior cells close to the border, from where the Dpp signal diffuses to the two compartments and controls their growth and pattern (Lawrence and Struhl, 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Lawrence and Struhl, 1996.

claim: The Dpp signal diffuses to the two compartments and controls their growth and pattern.
source: The posterior compartment cells secrete the Hedgehog (Hh) morphogen that activates the decapentaplegic (dpp) gene in the anterior cells close to the border, from where the Dpp signal diffuses to the two compartments and controls their growth and pattern (Lawrence and Struhl, 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Lawrence and Struhl, 1996.

claim: The Wg signal emanating from the D/V border has a major patterning function in the wing disc.
source: The Wg signal emanating from the D/V border also has a major patterning function in the wing disc (Irvine and Vogt, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Irvine and Vogt, 1997.

claim: The establishment and maintenance of the A/P and D/V boundaries are critical factors in the development of the wing disc.
source: It follows that the establishment and maintenance of the A/P and D/V boundaries are critical factors in the development of the wing disc and that major alterations of these boundaries would grossly interfere with normal pattern and growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the established roles of compartment boundaries.

claim: Major alterations of the A/P and D/V boundaries would grossly interfere with normal pattern and growth.
source: It follows that the establishment and maintenance of the A/P and D/V boundaries are critical factors in the development of the wing disc and that major alterations of these boundaries would grossly interfere with normal pattern and growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the established roles of compartment boundaries.

claim: Regenerative processes incorporate mechanisms to ensure the restoration of the A/P and D/V borders in damaged discs.
source: Therefore, it is expected that regenerative processes incorporate mechanisms to ensure the restoration of these borders in damaged discs.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the importance of compartment boundaries.

claim: The possibility of collapse and subsequent restoration of the A/P border during regeneration in the wing disc was suggested by Szabad et al. (1979).
source: The possibility of collapse and subsequent restoration of the A/P border during regeneration in the wing disc was suggested by Szabad et al. (1979), although recent reports (Bergantinos et al., 2010; Smith-Bolton et al., 2009) have failed to observe lineage transgressions after massive damage to the disc.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Szabad et al., 1979.

claim: Recent reports have failed to observe lineage transgressions after massive damage to the disc.
source: The possibility of collapse and subsequent restoration of the A/P border during regeneration in the wing disc was suggested by Szabad et al. (1979), although recent reports (Bergantinos et al., 2010; Smith-Bolton et al., 2009) have failed to observe lineage transgressions after massive damage to the disc.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bergantinos et al., 2010 and Smith-Bolton et al., 2009.

claim: Under experimental conditions (48 hr of continuous Flp activity) all the cells of the P compartment acquire the ßGal label.
source: Under our experimental conditions (48 hr of continuous Flp activity) all the cells of the P compartment acquire the ßGal label (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: After 48 hr of hid activity, the great majority of P compartment cells in the disc are dead or are dying.
source: After 48 hr of hid activity, the great majority of P compartment cells in the disc are dead or are dying (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: About 70% of the cells die after 48 hr of hid activity in the P compartment.
source: We estimate that about 70% of the cells die and as a result the size of the compartment is greatly reduced (compare Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is an estimate based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: The size of the P compartment is greatly reduced after 48 hr of hid activity.
source: We estimate that about 70% of the cells die and as a result the size of the compartment is greatly reduced (compare Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Despite massive cell death in the P compartment, there is a clear, although highly irregular, boundary separating anterior and posterior cells.
source: However, in spite of the massive cell death in the P compartment, there is clear, although highly irregular (Figure 1E–G), boundary separating anterior and posterior cells, outlined by the anterior compartment marker Ci.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: After allowing 72 hr of recovery at 17°C, the damaged P compartment is completely regenerated with normal size and shape and an almost normal A/P border.
source: After allowing 72 hr of recovery at 17°C, the damaged P compartment is completely regenerated: it exhibits normal size and shape and an almost normal A/P border.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the recovery experiments.

claim: The size of clones in the A and P compartment during the ablation period is similar.
source: The size of clones in the A and P compartment during the ablation period is similar (Figure 2A–D), although the P compartment clones have probably grown more since some of their cells must have died due to Hid activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the clonal analysis data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: P compartment clones have probably grown more during ablation since some of their cells must have died due to Hid activity.
source: The size of clones in the A and P compartment during the ablation period is similar (Figure 2A–D), although the P compartment clones have probably grown more since some of their cells must have died due to Hid activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that clone sizes are similar despite cell death.

claim: The proliferative response to ablation becomes evident during the recovery time.
source: The proliferative response to the ablation becomes evident during the recovery time (Figure 2E–H): clones in the P compartment are about 3 times bigger than those in the A compartment.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the clonal analysis data shown in Figure 2E-H.

claim: Clones in the P compartment during recovery are about 3 times bigger than those in the A compartment.
source: The proliferative response to the ablation becomes evident during the recovery time (Figure 2E–H): clones in the P compartment are about 3 times bigger than those in the A compartment.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the clonal analysis data shown in Figure 2E-H.

claim: Additional divisions during recovery restore the full size of the P compartment.
source: These additional divisions restore the full size of the compartment.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of increased proliferation and size restoration.

claim: The A and P compartments grow autonomously once the A/P border is re-established.
source: This result also illustrates the independent size regulation of the two compartments (Martin and Morata, 2006); once the A/P border is re-established the two compartments grow autonomously.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental results and citation to Martin and Morata, 2006.

claim: In the majority of discs in which the P compartment is ablated (22 out of 31), cells from the A compartment have contributed to the regenerated P compartment.
source: In the majority of discs in which the P compartment is ablated (22 out of 31), we find that cells from the A compartment have contributed to the regenerated P compartment.
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental observation.

claim: Transgressing cells from the A compartment are of anterior origin (lack ßGal staining) but now belong to the P compartment (lost Ci marker and gained en expression).
source: The transgressing cells are of anterior origin, as indicated by the lack of ßGal staining, but now belong to the P compartment, as showed by the lost the Ci anterior marker (Figure 3A) and the gain of en expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Lineage violations are not observed in control discs.
source: These lineage violations are not observed in control discs.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from control experiments.

claim: The transgressions localize to the proximity of the A/P border.
source: We find that the transgressions localize to the proximity of the A/P border (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), which argues strongly against that possibility.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Surviving cells from the ablated P compartment may contribute to the A compartment.
source: In addition, we unexpectedly find that surviving cells from the ablated P compartment may also contribute to the A compartment: cells of posterior provenance, labeled with ßGal, frequently penetrate (13 transgressions in a sample of 31 discs) into the A compartment and acquire anterior identity, visualized by ci activity (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental observation shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cells of posterior provenance frequently penetrate into the A compartment (13 transgressions in a sample of 31 discs) and acquire anterior identity.
source: In addition, we unexpectedly find that surviving cells from the ablated P compartment may also contribute to the A compartment: cells of posterior provenance, labeled with ßGal, frequently penetrate (13 transgressions in a sample of 31 discs) into the A compartment and acquire anterior identity, visualized by ci activity (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental observation shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The transgressions are caused by a transient collapse of the A/P boundary, which affects the two compartments.
source: Since the A compartment was not in need of reconstruction, this observation indicates that the transgressions are caused by a transient collapse of the A/P boundary, which affects the two compartments.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cells from both compartments cross the boundary.

claim: The A/P transgressions have occurred during the ablation period.
source: It is worth mentioning that the A/P transgressions have occurred during the ablation period, as they are found in discs fixed at the end of it, without recovery time (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, see also Figure 4E–E′′).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Figure 4E-E''.

claim: The restoration of the A/P border is immediate and concomitant with the ablation.
source: This is a significant observation because it suggests that the restoration of the A/P border is immediate and concomitant with the ablation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that transgressions occur during ablation.

claim: The lineage violations are not specific to the UAS-hid transgene.
source: The lineage violations are not specific to the UAS-hid transgene; we have made similar observations using other pro-apoptotic genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Numerous cases of clones crossing over the A/P border were found (10 cases of crossing in 16 discs examined).
source: As illustrated in Figure 3C, we found numerous cases of clones crossing over the A/P border (10 cases of crossing in 16 discs examined).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental observation shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Clones crossing the A/P border do not appear in discs of the same genotype in which the P compartment is not ablated.
source: These transgressions do not appear in discs of the same genotype in which the P compartment is not ablated.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from control experiments.

claim: A loss of lineage restriction was observed in the D/V compartment boundary after ablation of the D compartment.
source: A loss of lineage restriction was also observed in the D/V compartment boundary after ablation of the D compartment.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Cells of ventral provenance appear integrated in the regenerated D compartment and acquire PS1α integrin, a marker of dorsal cells.
source: We find that cells of ventral provenance appear integrated in the regenerated D compartment (Figure 3D). The change of identity is visualized by the acquisition by these cells of PS1α integrin, a marker of dorsal cells (Gotwals et al., 1994).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 3D and supported by citation to Gotwals et al., 1994.

claim: JNK signaling is involved in in situ regeneration in imaginal discs.
source: There is evidence that JNK signaling is involved in in situ regeneration in imaginal discs (Bergantinos et al., 2010; Herrera et al., 2013; Worley et al., 2012) and also in transdetermination of transplanted discs (Lee et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Bergantinos et al., 2010; Herrera et al., 2013; Worley et al., 2012; and Lee et al., 2005.

claim: JNK activity is required for the change of en expression and subsequent crossing of the A/P border by some cells during dorsal closure in Drosophila embryos.
source: Moreover, a recent report (Gettings et al., 2010) indicates that JNK activity is required for the change of en expression and subsequent crossing of the A/P border by some cells during dorsal closure in Drosophila embryos.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gettings et al., 2010.

claim: JNK is up regulated in the P compartments of ablated hh > hid discs, as shown by the activation of the puc-LacZ marker.
source: We had previously noticed that JNK is up regulated in the P compartments of ablated hh > hid discs, as shown by the activation of the puc-LacZ marker, which is not normally expressed in the wing pouch (Figure 4B,B′).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 4B,B'.

claim: Anterior compartment cells near the A/P border express the puc-LacZ marker after ablation.
source: This was expected because Hid induces JNK (Shlevkov and Morata, 2012), but we also find anterior compartment cells near the A/P border that express the puc-LacZ marker (Figure 4A–A′′).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 4A-A'' and supported by citation to Shlevkov and Morata, 2012.

claim: In experimental discs where JNK activation is prevented in the P compartment, the A/P transgressions are greatly reduced.
source: In the experimental discs, the transgressions are greatly reduced, clearly indicating a requirement for JNK function.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: JNK function is required for A/P lineage transgressions.
source: In the experimental discs, the transgressions are greatly reduced, clearly indicating a requirement for JNK function.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental manipulation of JNK activity.

claim: A/P transgressions occur after damage to the A compartment, even if only a portion of the compartment is affected.
source: This experiment also shows that A/P transgressions also occur after damage to the A compartment, even if only a portion of the compartment is affected.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental results from the dpp-LHG experiment.

claim: After ablation of the dorsal compartment, the expression of engrailed in the dorsal part of the posterior compartment is lower than in the corresponding region in the ventral compartment.
source: In support of this, we observe that after ablation of the dorsal compartment (in ap>hid discs, Figure 5—figure supplement 2) the expression of engrailed in the dorsal part of the posterior compartment is lower than in the corresponding region in the ventral compartment.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Pc-G genes are responsible for keeping in off state (silencing) the genes inappropriate for a particular identity.
source: The Pc-G genes are responsible for keeping in off state (silencing) the genes inappropriate for a particular identity, whereas the trx-G genes maintain the activity of identity-specific genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of Pc-G genes.

claim: The trx-G genes maintain the activity of identity-specific genes.
source: The Pc-G genes are responsible for keeping in off state (silencing) the genes inappropriate for a particular identity, whereas the trx-G genes maintain the activity of identity-specific genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of trx-G genes.

claim: The Pc-G and trx-G genes control en expression in the A and P compartments.
source: It is known that the Pc-G and trx-G genes control en expression in the A and P compartments (Busturia and Morata, 1988; Breen et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Busturia and Morata, 1988 and Breen et al., 1995.

claim: In Pc3/+ discs, the number and size of lineage transgressions is greatly increased with respect to controls.
source: The results indicate an involvement of the Pc-G and trx-G genes (Figure 5A–G): in Pc3/+ discs, the number and size of lineage transgressions is greatly increased with respect to controls, whereas in trxE2/+ discs there are very few lineage transgressions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 5A-G.

claim: In trxE2/+ discs there are very few lineage transgressions.
source: The results indicate an involvement of the Pc-G and trx-G genes (Figure 5A–G): in Pc3/+ discs, the number and size of lineage transgressions is greatly increased with respect to controls, whereas in trxE2/+ discs there are very few lineage transgressions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 5A-G.

claim: In discs in which the P compartment is ablated there is a clear down regulation of Psc activity.
source: In Psc-QF>QUAS-mtdTomato discs in which the P compartment is ablated there is a clear down regulation of Psc activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: There is an increase in the levels of tri-methylation of H3K4, a mark of active chromatin, after P compartment ablation.
source: We also find an increase in the levels of tri-methylation of H3K4, a mark of active chromatin (Schubeler et al., 2004) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D and supported by citation to Schubeler et al., 2004.

claim: The modifications in Psc and H3K4 affect the entire posterior compartment and the region of the A compartment close to the A/P border.
source: In both cases, the modifications affect the entire posterior compartment and the region of the A compartment close to the A/P border.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data on epigenetic markers.

claim: The changes of identity during regeneration are associated with temporal relaxation of the epigenetic control of compartment identity.
source: Taking everything together the preceding results strongly suggest that the changes of identity during regeneration are associated with temporal relaxation of the epigenetic control of compartment identity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on Pc-G, trx-G, and epigenetic markers.

claim: Cells in the neighborhood of the A/P (or D/V) boundary may lose some of their developmental constraints during regeneration, thus descending to a kind of 'naive' (undetermined) state.
source: We conjecture that as a result cells in the neighborhood of the A/P (or D/V) boundary may lose some of their developmental constraints, thus descending to a kind of 'naive' (undetermined) state.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Identity changes observed appear to be influenced by the local developmental context.
source: The reason behind this speculation was the realization that identity changes observed appear to be influenced by the local developmental context, that is, the cells may change from anterior to posterior, but keep the overall wing identity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cells maintain wing identity while changing compartment identity.

claim: Dorsal compartment cells expressing en appear to induce the en-LacZ reporter in ventral cells located in their vicinity.
source: There is a recent observation (Garaulet et al., 2008) that dorsal compartment cells expressing en appear to induce the en-LacZ reporter in ventral cells located in their vicinity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Garaulet et al., 2008.

claim: Unmarked anterior cells surrounded by en-expressing clones often activate the endogenous en gene.
source: We find that these unmarked cells often activate the endogenous en gene, as indicated by the expression of the en-lacZ insert (Figure 6C–E′′) and also by the presence of the En protein (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B′′).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6C-E'' and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B''.

claim: The gain of en activity in anterior cells is associated with down regulation of the A compartment markers Ci and Ptc.
source: The gain of en activity is associated with down regulation of the A compartment markers Ci and Ptc (Figure 6D′′,E′′, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–D′′).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6D'',E'' and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D''.

claim: En activation in anterior cells only occurs in discs densely populated by en-expressing clones.
source: Significantly, this activation only occurs in discs densely populated by en-expressing clones; it does not appear if there are few clones (Figure 6A–B′′).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6A-B''.

claim: The induction process requires the receiving cells to be largely surrounded by inducing cells.
source: It suggests that the induction process requires the receiving cells to be largely surrounded by inducing cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that induction only occurs with high clone density.

claim: En is non-autonomously activated at 17°C where the levels of en over-expression in the clones are lower.
source: This experiment was also performed at 17°C, a temperature at which the Gal4 system is less active and therefore the levels of en over-expression in the clones are lower. The result (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) is that en is also non-autonomously activated under these conditions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Clones in the anterior compartment expressing Gal80 and surrounded by cells with high levels of en activity show induction of endogenous en activity.
source: In these clones, we also observe induction of endogenous en activity (Figure 6F–G′).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6F-G'.

claim: The phenomenon of en induction is not due to the Hedgehog-mediated late activation of en in the anterior cells close to the A/P border.
source: We believe that the phenomenon of en induction it is not due to the Hedgehog -mediated late activation of en in the anterior cells close to the A/P border (Blair, 1992), because the en-lacZ insert line we use in these experiments does not show this effect (Figure 6H,H′).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 6H,H' and citation to Blair, 1992.

claim: En induction is only observed in discs densely populated by en-expressing clones; in discs with fewer clones it does not occur.
source: Furthermore, as noted above, we only observe en induction in discs densely populated by en-expressing clones; in discs with fewer clones it does not occur (compare A–B′′ and C–D′′ panels in Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The Hh-mediated activation of en would not depend on clone density.
source: The Hh-mediated activation would not depend on clone density.
evidence: This is inferred from knowledge about Hh signaling mechanisms.

claim: The P compartment fully regenerates after a massive damage that kills the majority of the cells.
source: We find that the P compartment fully regenerates after a massive damage that kills the majority of the cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental results.

claim: There is a proliferative response aimed to restore the normal size of the P compartment.
source: There is a proliferative response aimed to restore the normal size of the compartment (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the clonal analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The proliferative response may start during the ablation period.
source: This response is easily visualized during post-ablation time (Figure 2E–H), although it may start during the ablation: the fact that clones in the P compartment, which is under ablation, grow as much as those in the control A compartment (Figure 2A–D) suggests that they perform more cell divisions.
evidence: This is inferred from the clonal analysis data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: The autonomous proliferative response of the A and P compartment provides evidence that A and P compartments are units of growth control.
source: The autonomous proliferative response of the A and P compartment provides further evidence to the proposal that A and P compartments are units of growth control (Martin and Morata, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental results and citation to Martin and Morata, 2006.

claim: The collapse of the boundary results from a transient loss (or debilitation) of the identity of cells in the P compartment and likely some anterior cells close to the border.
source: Possibly, the collapse of the boundary results from a transient loss (or debilitation) of the identity of cells in the P compartment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and likely some anterior cells close to the border (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claim: As a consequence of identity loss, posterior cells can mix with juxtaposing anterior cells, in effect eliminating the boundary.
source: As a consequence posterior cells can mix with juxtaposing anterior cells, in effect eliminating the boundary.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of boundary collapse and cell mixing.

claim: The behavior of the posterior cells derives from a diminution of en activity, responsible for posterior identity and for maintaining the A/P border.
source: We believe the behavior of the posterior cells derives from a diminution of en activity, responsible for posterior identity and for maintaining the A/P border (Morata and Lawrence, 1975).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations and supported by citation to Morata and Lawrence, 1975.

claim: The diminution of en activity appears to be caused by attenuation of the control exerted by the Pc-G and trx-G genes and up regulation of the JNK pathway.
source: In turn, it appears to be caused by two factors: attenuation of the control exerted by the Pc-G and trx-G genes (Figure 5), and up regulation of the JNK pathway (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figures 4A and 5.

claim: The Pc-G and trx-G genes and the JNK pathway are known to be involved in controlling en activity.
source: These two pathways are known to be involved in controlling en activity (Busturia and Morata, 1988; Breen et al., 1995; Gettings et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Busturia and Morata, 1988; Breen et al., 1995; and Gettings et al., 2010.

claim: The collapse of the boundary is followed by a very rapid reconstruction.
source: We observe that the collapse of the boundary is followed by a very rapid reconstruction.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: There is a functional A/P border after 48 hr of ablation without allowing time for recovery.
source: The fact that there is a functional A/P border after 48 hr of ablation and without allowing time for recovery (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, also Figure 4E), strongly suggests an immediate re-establishment.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Figure 4E.

claim: The reconstruction of the A/P border results from the acquisition of new anterior or posterior identities by the cells close to the border.
source: The reconstruction must result from the acquisition of new anterior or posterior identities by the cells close to the border.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of boundary reconstruction and identity changes.

claim: Islands of anterior cells in which en is originally inactive are induced to activate the gene when surrounded by en-expressing cells.
source: We believe that the mechanism behind this reprogramming is the phenomenon of gene induction by neighbors that we report here (Figure 6A–H′): islands of anterior cells in which en is originally inactive are induced to activate the gene when surrounded by en-expressing cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6A-H'.

claim: In the developmental context of the wing disc, the cells around the A/P border only have the option of being en-on or en-off, depending on the active genotype of surrounding cells.
source: In the developmental context of the wing disc, the cells around the A/P border only have the option of being en-on or en-off, depending on the active genotype of surrounding cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations and the developmental context.

claim: Many developmental decisions in Drosophila are taken collectively by small groups of cells.
source: In Drosophila many developmental decisions are taken collectively by small groups of cells: the compartmental subdivisions occur in groups of cells (Garcia-Bellido et al., 1973).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Garcia-Bellido et al., 1973.

claim: The phenomenon of 'transdetermination' in which cells change their original segmental determination in transplantation experiments is not a clonal but a collective decision.
source: Similarly, the phenomenon of 'transdetermination' in which cells change their original segmental determination in transplantation experiments (Gehring, 1967), is not a clonal but a collective decision.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Gehring, 1967.

claim: Group interactions to generate a coherent pattern of development resemble the 'community effect' described by John Gurdon.
source: These group interactions to generate a coherent pattern of developmental resemble the 'community effect' described by John Gurdon years ago (Gurdon, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gurdon, 1988.

claim: Induction by neighbors may be part of a group decision process during normal development.
source: One could speculate that induction by neighbors may be part of a group decision process during normal development.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The initial activation of en during embryogenesis is induced by the transcription factors eve and ftz.
source: The initial activation of en during embryogenesis is induced by the transcription factors eve and ftz (DiNardo et al., 1988).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to DiNardo et al., 1988.

claim: Not all cells respond similarly to Eve or Ftz during initial en activation.
source: It is possible that not all the cells respond similarly to Eve or Ftz—it is known that the initial en expression is inhomogeneous (DiNardo et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to DiNardo et al., 1985.

claim: Secondary induction via the local context would ensure the coherent activation of engrailed in the entire group.
source: The secondary induction via the local context would ensure the coherent activation of engrailed in the entire group.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the induction by neighbors phenomenon.

claim: The En protein may act as a short-range signal.
source: There is a recent report suggesting the possibility that the En protein may act as a short-range signal (Layalle et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Layalle et al., 2011.

claim: The En product itself may activate en non-autonomously.
source: It raises the possibility that the En product itself may activate en non-autonomously.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the citation to Layalle et al., 2011.
